question: Why did customers who left decide to leave?

resolution.read_instruction: Extract every stated reason the customer gave for leaving or considering leaving OrbitFlow, including product gaps, pricing or budget, support issues, switching to a competitor, internal changes, and any OrbitFlow staff explanations or concessions about those reasons.
assumptions: 'Customers who left' maps to the Churn post-mortem call type.
Question asks about the reasons for churn across all churn post-mortem calls, not a single named company.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Properly? June.
findings.context: Customer decided to leave in June; the decision was inevitable from about February. — Timeline of when the decision was made; customer says it took until June to admit it.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Our settlement provider is a mid-sized European processor. You don't have a connector for them. Nobody does, to be fair — Workato doesn't either.
findings.context: The settlement reconciliation workflow could not be built on OrbitFlow because the settlement provider has no connector and the effort exceeded value. — Sarah frames the February failure as effort exceeding value; she also says Workato lacks a connector too, so the connector gap was not the differentiator.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: The connector gap was real. But it wasn't why we left. It was the thing we pointed at.
findings.context: The real reason for leaving was that business users never built workflows; the platform was used as an engineering tool, not worth the premium paid for a business-user platform. — Kwame explicitly says the connector gap was not why they left; the reason was the unmet business-user autonomy pitch. Stated reason (connector gap) differs from the real reason per the customer.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Two years in, every single production workflow was built by Sarah's team.
findings.context: Every production workflow was built by engineering, and the business-user model did not materialise. — Customer's account of why the value was not realised.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Because we were maintaining custom integrations to a platform whose main selling point was that we wouldn't have to maintain custom integrations.
findings.context: Licence cost was being justified by business-user autonomy that wasn't materialising, and they were maintaining custom integrations despite the platform promising they wouldn't need to. — Engineering manager's reasons for supporting departure.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: two of my engineers wanted to build it in-house and I spent eighteen months arguing against them, and eventually I ran out of arguments.
findings.context: Engineers wanted to build in-house, and the maintenance argument eventually lost; the customer chose Workato, which is an engineering-oriented tool. — Internal engineering pressure contributed to the departure.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Less. Not dramatically less.
findings.context: Price was not the primary reason for leaving; Workato was only slightly cheaper. — Customer rejects price as the primary driver, though it was partly a factor at the margin.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: Their connector for our core banking platform is genuinely better than yours. That one's just true.
findings.context: Workato was chosen over OrbitFlow because of a stronger core banking connector and a stronger engineering-facing story. — Competitor advantages cited by customer; OrbitFlow staff acknowledged the connector point.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: Then you've designed a product that fails by default for people like me.
findings.context: Enablement was insufficient: a two-day onboarding with eight attendees, six never returned, and OrbitFlow's paid hands-on services were never offered until January, after the customer had decided. — OrbitFlow staff acknowledged the paid professional services engagement exists and that the product may fail by default without it.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Then we don't say it, do we.
findings.context: The product does not remove the need for a dedicated operations automation role; it changes what the role must be good at. OrbitFlow staff said this is in operating model guidance, but the customer had never seen it. — Root gap identified: no dedicated role owned automation at Verity.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: It's not why we left. But it contributed to a general feeling that we were a small account.
findings.context: Support was inconsistent and the account felt small; Ruth acknowledged the account was below median and treated as small, though support was not the reason for leaving. — Customer explicitly says support was not why they left but contributed to feeling like a small account.

findings.speaker: Sarah Lindqvist
findings.quote: That's when it was over, if you want the specific moment.
findings.context: Customer felt the April connector problem during the Workato evaluation was resolved by a free SE build, while OrbitFlow's response was only a no-template answer; this moment ended the OrbitFlow relationship. — Competitor concession shifted momentum; OrbitFlow staff unlikely to have argued for similar support given account size.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: By March we'd started the Workato evaluation and once that starts it has its own momentum.
findings.context: Once the Workato evaluation started by March it had its own momentum, so little could have been done in the last six months. — Customer's view that the decision was locked in by evaluation dynamics.

findings.speaker: Kwame Boateng
findings.quote: if someone had sat with two of my people for a week in the first quarter and got them to ship something real, we'd still be a customer.
findings.context: Customer would have stayed if someone had sat with two operations people for a week in Q1 to ship a real workflow; Kwame also says he declined January sessions because he had already half-concluded it would not work. — Stated counterfactual and a self-admitted reason for declining the sessions.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We bought something we didn't need. That's the whole answer.
findings.context: Customer left because they bought a plan larger than they needed; the purchase was not matched to actual usage. — Primary stated reason for churn; customer says product is fine, the problem is over-purchase (Growth plan, 30 users, 4 active).

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We were on Growth, at eighteen hundred a month, for thirty users, when we had four people who ever logged in.
findings.context: Cost driver: Growth plan at £1,800/month for 30 users while only four people ever logged in. — Pricing/budget reason; customer contrasts plan size with actual usage.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: About two thousand a year. Maybe two and a half with the tier we need.
findings.context: Customer is moving to Zapier at roughly a tenth of the cost, about £2,000–£2,500 a year. — Switching to a competitor, driven by price; customer had used Zapier before.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: They worked perfectly. That's the frustrating part. I've got no complaint about the product at all.
findings.context: Customer says the product works well and has no complaint about it; the departure is not about product quality. — Explicitly separates product satisfaction from the reason for leaving.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We'll lose the approval steps and we'll lose the run history, which I'll genuinely miss.
findings.context: Features lost by switching to Zapier: approval forms and run history, which the customer will miss. — Customer acknowledges trade-off; approval forms are needed for contractor sign-off and Zapier cannot do them well.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: We paid for eleven workflows' worth of value and a plan for forty.
findings.context: Promised scaling roadmap (compliance, service charges, contractor management) never happened because the company lacked capacity; the purchase was priced against a future that did not occur. — Internal capacity change/adoption gap; both sides were enthusiastic during sales.

findings.speaker: Alastair McCrae
findings.quote: I probably should have pushed harder on whether you had the capacity for the roadmap we talked about.
findings.context: OrbitFlow staff acknowledged the account was over-sized and nobody checked capacity for the roadmap; no one acted on low usage. — Vendor concession about missed usage monitoring and roadmap fit.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: If you'd had something at five or six hundred a month I'd still be a customer
findings.context: Customer wanted a smaller entry plan (around £500–600/month); none exists, so they could not downsize and left. — Product/packaging gap; customer says a smaller plan would have retained them.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: With the approval forms, yes. Without them, no
findings.context: Customer would not buy a smaller plan without approval forms, so the approval forms are the key retained feature. — Conditional interest in a downsell; approval forms are the deciding feature.

findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi
findings.quote: Your account was in a segment that doesn't get an assigned CSM.
findings.context: Vendor's account was in a segment with no assigned CSM, so low usage was not noticed and no one reached out beyond a product announcement. — Vendor explanation for lack of early intervention; customer links it to missed warning signs.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: The problem being solved becomes invisible. Exactly that. Nobody remembers how bad it was.
findings.context: Value faded over time: after a year the pain the product solved stopped feeling urgent while the invoice kept arriving, prompting a renewal review. — Gradual value erosion at renewal; customer says nothing broke.

findings.speaker: Hazel Wren
findings.quote: nineteen thousand pounds is a member of staff for four months
findings.context: Customer's decision was driven by a budget case: £19,000 a year equated to a staff member for four months, which the MD accepted. — Budget justification for leaving.

rejected_findings.claim: OrbitFlow staff say a paid services engagement exists; the customer had not been offered it until the January visit.
rejected_findings.quote: It's a paid professional services engagement.
rejected_findings.speaker: Ruth Adeyemi

draft.answer: The two churned customers left for different reasons. Oakhill Property left mainly because it had bought an oversized plan and found a far cheaper option in Zapier [C1][C2][C3]. Verity Payments says the real reason was that business users never built workflows, even though the connector gap was what they pointed at [C4][C5][C6]. Both calls also show OrbitFlow missing early warning signs [C7][C8].

claims.text: Oakhill Property (Hazel Wren) said they left because they bought a plan larger than needed: Growth at £1,800/month for 30 users, with only four people ever logging in. She said the product worked perfectly and she has no complaint about it.

Oakhill is moving to Zapier for about £2,000–£2,500 a year, roughly a tenth of the cost. The budget case was that £19,000 a year equals a staff member for four months. They will lose approval forms and run history.

Oakhill's scaling roadmap (compliance, service charges, contractor management) never happened for lack of capacity. Value also faded over time as the problem being solved stopped feeling urgent while the invoice kept arriving. No smaller plan existed (Hazel would have stayed at about £500–600/month, but only with approval forms).

Verity Payments' Kwame Boateng said the connector gap was real but not why they left; it was 'the thing we pointed at'. The real reason was that business users never built workflows: every production workflow was built by engineering, so the premium was not justified.

Verity's contributing factors: engineers wanted to build in-house and Sarah Lindqvist ran out of arguments; Workato had a better core banking connector and a stronger engineering-facing story; the onboarding was thin (two days, six of eight attendees never returned) and paid services were offered only in January after the decision. Kwame said Verity would have stayed if someone had sat with two operations people for a week in Q1 to ship a real workflow.

Verity's decision timeline: the decision was effectively made around February but admitted in June. The Workato evaluation was under way by March and had its own momentum. Sarah said the specific moment it was over was when a free SE build by Workato fixed the April connector problem while OrbitFlow offered only a no-template answer. Price was not the primary reason (Workato was only slightly cheaper), and support was not the reason but made them feel like a small account.
Oakhill's account was in a segment with no assigned CSM, so low usage went unnoticed. Alastair McCrae acknowledged he should have pushed harder on whether Oakhill had the capacity for the roadmap.

Ruth Adeyemi acknowledged that Verity's account was below median and treated as small. The need for a dedicated operations automation role is in the operating model guidance, but the customer had never seen it.

conflicts.topic: Verity: stated vs real reason for leaving
conflicts.description: Verity pointed to the connector gap (the settlement provider connector, and Workato's better core banking connector), but Kwame said it was not why they left; the real reason was the unmet business-user autonomy promise. Sarah also noted Workato lacks the settlement connector too.
